messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 32
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Housekeeper
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 61

He is a 32-year-old South Asian man who works as a housekeeper and has built his life around routines that keep him moving and useful. Before the assault, he describes himself as someone who got up early, took pride in leaving rooms spotless, and tried to stay out of trouble. He has been married for several years, and he and his wife had been talking about saving for a better apartment. He recalls feeling tired much of the time from work, but steady. He says he was the kind of person who did not like conflict and believed that if he kept his head down, life would leave him alone.

The mugging happens on an ordinary evening as he is walking home after finishing a late shift. He is carrying a small bag with his lunch container, keys, and the wages he has just picked up. He remembers the street being quiet, the air cold, and his attention on getting home to his wife. Then two men step into his path. One has a knife, though he does not understand that at first; he remembers only the flash of metal and the sudden feeling that his body is no longer his own. They demand his wallet and phone. He gives them what he has without thinking, but one of them shoves him hard against a wall, and the impact knocks the breath out of him. He says time seems to break apart in pieces: the sound of their voices, the scrape of shoes, his own heart pounding so violently that he thinks he may vomit. He is struck once, maybe twice, and then they are gone. He stands frozen long after they run off, unable to move, embarrassed by how helpless he feels.

In the first days afterward, he tells himself he should be grateful that he survived. He goes back to work because he needs the money and because staying home feels worse. But he is no longer able to move through the world in the same way. He begins scanning every corner, every parked car, every person walking behind him. When a door slams or someone raises a hand too quickly, his body jolts before his mind catches up. He says he feels as if the attack is still happening somewhere nearby, just out of sight. On his route home, he changes streets repeatedly, even if it makes him late. He starts checking over his shoulder several times before stepping out of a bus or turning onto a dark block.

At work, where he once found comfort in the predictable tasks of making beds and cleaning bathrooms, he becomes tense and watchful. He double-checks locks, keeps his phone in his hand, and does not like being alone in hallways. When he hears footsteps approaching from behind, his chest tightens and his mouth goes dry. He finds himself startling at the metallic clatter of carts or the sudden opening of guestroom doors. He wants to appear calm in front of coworkers, but inside he feels constantly braced, as if waiting for another blow. He notices that he sleeps lightly and wakes at the smallest noise. Some nights he dreams of being cornered, though he usually wakes before the worst part of the dream becomes clear. He lies in bed afterward, staring into the dark, listening to the sounds of the building and wondering whether the men will somehow return.

He does not talk about the mugging easily. His wife tries to ask, but he gives short answers and changes the subject. He feels ashamed that he could not fight back and ashamed again that he still feels afraid. He says the shame makes him quieter, less present at home. He eats less when he is upset and sometimes loses track of time while sitting on the couch, replaying the moment the men stepped toward him. He imagines different endings: what if he had taken another street, what if he had run, what if he had shouted. These thoughts circle without giving him relief. Instead, they leave him irritated and exhausted. Even small frustrations at work now feel hard to manage, and he notices himself snapping inwardly when someone interrupts him or asks one question too many.

Over time, he becomes more careful, but not more relaxed. He avoids going out after dark unless absolutely necessary and prefers to be accompanied when he can manage it. He keeps to well-lit places and feels uneasy in crowds, where he cannot predict who is near him or where they are standing. He remains devoted to his wife, yet he says the attack has changed the way he inhabits his own life. He is still working, still paying bills, still keeping his home in order, but he moves through each day with a sense that danger is closer than it should be.
